# Proposal

## Milestone 1: A minimal metadata schema

We will begin with eight required fields: identifier, title, source URL, lesson URL, engine or format, maintainer, license, and learning objectives. We will map these fields to Schema.org and the Bioschemas TrainingMaterial profile where applicable. Topic, level, prerequisites, packages, deployment mode, duration, accessibility information, and software versions will be optional in the initial schema. Missing values will be explicit; fields needed for a particular check must be supplied or inferred reliably by its adapter before that check can run. Validation dates and results will be generated by the checking tools. Nominations with unknown maintainers or licenses will remain pending review.

We will reuse metadata already present in tutorial sources and use a small accompanying file for missing fields. Authors will not need to rewrite lessons. Engine maintainers and educators will review the draft schema, and the pilot will test the effort needed to describe existing tutorials before version 1.0. We will publish the schema, example records, and adoption guidance.

## Milestone 2: Adapters for existing engines

Adapters will translate each engine's metadata and available checks into the common format. Proposed interfaces include `learnr_adapter()`, `learnr2_adapter()`, and `quarto_adapter()`, with Quarto Live support in the Quarto adapter. We will refine the interfaces with maintainers and document the versions and features each adapter supports.

An adapter may invoke an engine's existing build or checking tools, but will not implement its execution system or promise conversion between engines. A capability table will distinguish metadata import, rendering checks, code execution, and accessibility checks. Carpentries-style materials can enter the registry through common metadata and link checks; deeper checks will depend on their build system. This lets the registry include useful resources without implying identical test coverage.

## Milestone 3: Validation across engines

`check_tutorial()` will combine common checks with the selected adapter. It will check metadata, links, and required files, then assess declared dependencies and package versions. Where the engine supports it, the adapter will test rendering and executable code and identify missing or duplicate exercise identifiers. Basic automated accessibility checks will accompany human review of keyboard use and instructional clarity.

Reports will identify the failing field or exercise and record the tested environment, source version, and date. Reports will distinguish unsupported or unrun checks from passes and failures across all engines. A reachable page, a successful render, or precomputed output will not count as testing interactive exercises. Passing automated checks will not establish teaching quality or full accessibility.

We will publish a reusable GitHub Actions workflow and integration guidance so authors can run checks in their own repositories without joining the registry. We will test the package on Linux, macOS, and Windows, using examples with known faults to verify that the checks detect problems.

## Milestone 4: A registry of independently maintained tutorials

The registry will index tutorial descriptions and link to the original repositories and published lessons. Authors will retain responsibility for their content and hosting. Each registry entry will be a YAML file, with automated ingestion into a searchable website and a published `index.json`. A proposed `tutorial_search()` function will return results as an R data frame.

Readers will filter by topic, package, level, learning objective, engine, and deployment mode where those fields are available. Duration and maintenance status will provide further context where available. Entries will distinguish metadata validity, execution checks, and human review so readers can judge the evidence available for a tutorial. Scheduled checks will flag broken links and outdated validation records.

The initial pilot will index 5–10 existing tutorials across the supported formats. We will record missing fields and manual corrections to assess the effort required from authors. Acceptance will require valid records and working search results, while execution claims will depend on separate adapter tests.

## Milestone 5: Review, governance, and example tutorials

Authors will submit entries through structured pull requests, and others will be able to nominate tutorials. Automated checks will precede human review of instructional clarity, accessibility, scope, licensing, and maintenance expectations. Review criteria will draw on open lesson-review practices [@carpentrieslab2022]. Published guidance will distinguish nominations from author submissions and explain corrections, removal, and archival decisions. Governance documentation will name responsibilities for maintaining the schema, package, and registry.

We will use four small example tutorials to test the adapters: renv, package development with usethis and devtools, an introductory DESeq2 workflow, and a Carpentries R companion. We will choose representative exercises and adapt existing material under compatible licenses. Bharti's r-for-beginners lessons and Bioconductor training resources offer starting points.

These tutorials will test metadata mapping, validation reports, and engine-specific checks as development proceeds. Together they will cover the three initial adapters; we will not require every example to run under every engine. Tests will include browser interaction where supported and local or server execution where needed. Three or four small integration templates will show authors how to connect their chosen engine to tutorialverse using their existing lessons.
